messages.subject: Re: chiroptera
parts:
> > I am going to begin to work in the estimation of the
> > abundance and density of urban bats in my city.
> > I am going to look for roots with the point sampling
> > and to use the program of Distance 4.

If you plan to record flying bats from points, that will not work if the
aim is to estimate absolute abundance, because point transect sampling
seriously overestimates abundance if the animals are moving around to the
extent that flying bats do. To avoid this, you need to be able to take a
'snapshot' from each point (see 2001 distance sampling book). I'm not
sure if this will be feasible in your study. (Sample size can be enhanced
by taking a series of snapshots at each point, perhaps with a few minutes
between each. The distances to each bat at each snapshot moment can then
be pooled, and effort at the point recorded as the number of snapshot
moments at that point.

If these methods are not workable, you may have to just resort to a
relative index of abundance. Often for bats, bat 'passes' are counted,
using bat detectors. In this case, it is often difficult or impossible to
get distance data, and to determine how many different bats were detected.
Also, snapshot methods don't work well when relying on bat detectors.
Bat detectors do allow identification of species, which can be problematic
for visual detections.

If anyone has developed reliable line or point transect methods for bats,
I would be interested to hear, as these seem a particularly difficult
group of species!

Steve Buckland
